wrong_text: Mine 7, just outside Longyearbyen, still produces around 100,000 tonnes of coal a year, supplying the local power station.
problem: Mine 7 permanently closed in June/July 2025 — it is no longer operating. The lesson presents it as a current, ongoing operation. Students citing this as a live example in 2026 exams would be factually wrong. Source: multiple news sources including Polar Journal, High North News, Global Energy Monitor.
correction: Mine 7, just outside Longyearbyen, produced around 100,000 tonnes of coal a year before its closure in 2025, supplying the local power station.

wrong_text: The international <dfn class="term" data-def="The 1991 treaty signed by 54 nations committing to preserve Antarctica for peaceful and scientific purposes, banning military activity and mineral extraction.">Antarctic Treaty</dfn> (1959, 54 nations) goes further, banning all mineral extraction in Antarctica entirely and designating it as a scientific preserve.
problem: Two errors here. (1) The 1959 Antarctic Treaty did NOT ban mining — it was the 1991 Madrid Protocol (Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty) that introduced the mining ban. Attributing the mining ban to the 1959 treaty is factually wrong and could cost marks. (2) '54 nations' is outdated — as of 2024 the treaty has 58 parties (ats.aq). The 54-nation figure was accurate circa 2011–2019.
correction: The international <dfn class="term" data-def="The 1959 treaty, supplemented by the 1991 Madrid Protocol, committing nations to preserve Antarctica for peaceful and scientific purposes, banning military activity and mineral extraction.">Antarctic Treaty</dfn> (1959, now 58 parties) goes further — its 1991 Madrid Protocol bans all mineral extraction in Antarctica entirely and designates it as a scientific preserve.

wrong_text: The 1959 treaty signed by 54 nations committing to preserve Antarctica for peaceful and scientific purposes, banning military activity and mineral extraction.
problem: Same two errors as the dfn in content_html: (1) the mining ban comes from the 1991 Madrid Protocol, not the original 1959 treaty; (2) '54 nations' is outdated — 58 parties as of 2024. The glossary definition is what students memorise verbatim.
correction: The 1959 treaty (extended by the 1991 Madrid Protocol) committing nations to preserve Antarctica for peaceful and scientific purposes, banning military activity and mineral extraction.

wrong_text: Russia operates the settlement of Barentsburg (population around 500) under this treaty. Norway wants to expand protected areas and reduce coal mining, but cannot simply exclude other nations from the islands.
problem: The claim that Norway 'cannot simply exclude other nations' from coal mining is slightly undermined by Mine 7's actual 2025 closure, which happened under Norwegian decision. However the broader treaty-tension framing is accurate. No factual number error here — Barentsburg ~500 is consistent with cited figures. No change needed; included for awareness only.
correction: No change required — Barentsburg population figure and treaty tension description are accurate.

wrong_text: It grants Norway sovereignty but gives all 46 signatory nations the right to carry out commercial activities.
problem: The Svalbard Treaty currently has 48 parties (as of 2025, per the Norwegian Storting); Turkey acceded in 2024 bringing it to 48, and the UAE became the 49th in April 2026. The figure '46' is out of date. Students should use the figure cited in their textbook, but '46' will be marked wrong if cross-referenced against a current source.
correction: It grants Norway sovereignty but gives all signatory nations (currently around 46–49, depending on the year) the right to carry out commercial activities.

wrong_text: the 1920 Svalbard Treaty gives Norway sovereignty but guarantees other signatory nations — including Russia, the USA and the UK — the right to carry out commercial activities.
problem: This phrasing is accurate — no signatory count given here, so no number error. The named examples (Russia, USA, UK) are correct. No change needed.

wrong_text: Mine 7, near Longyearbyen, producing around 100,000 tonnes per year
problem: Match-question answer describes Mine 7 as currently producing — Mine 7 closed June/July 2025. The answer needs past-tense correction to match the content_html fix.
correction: Mine 7, near Longyearbyen, which produced around 100,000 tonnes of coal per year before its closure in 2025

wrong_text: Mine 7, near Longyearbyen, producing around 100,000 tonnes per year.
problem: Same Mine 7 closure issue — flashcard presents it as current. Students memorising this will recall an incorrect 'live' operation.
correction: Mine 7, near Longyearbyen, which produced around 100,000 tonnes per year before closing in 2025.

wrong_text: mineral extraction (Mine 7 coal, around 100,000 tonnes per year)
problem: Mark scheme answer describes Mine 7 as a current operation. Needs past-tense correction.
correction: mineral extraction (Mine 7 coal, ~100,000 tonnes per year before its 2025 closure)

wrong_text: Mine 7 produces roughly 100,000 tonnes of coal annually.
problem: Mine 7 closed June/July 2025 — present tense is wrong.
correction: Mine 7 produced roughly 100,000 tonnes of coal annually before closing in 2025.

problem: Mine 7 has closed — framing it as a current opportunity is misleading. The bullet should acknowledge the closure or shift to past tense.
correction: mineral extraction (Mine 7 coal, now closed — operated until 2025)

problem: Exam tip tells students to cite 'Mine 7' as a statistic for an exam answer. As Mine 7 has closed, students should note it as a historical rather than current example to avoid examiner challenge. The statistic itself (100,000 t/yr) is still useable as a past figure.
correction: No full replacement needed but add '(now closed, operated until 2025)' after 'Mine 7' so students contextualise correctly.
